chemical: Silver tip-Green tip stage: Mancozeb (400 g) or Captan (300 g) per 100 litres water
Pink bud stage: Contaf (30 ml) or Baycor (50 g) per 100 litres water
Petal fall stage: Bavistin (50 g) or Topsin M (50 g) per 100 litres water
Pea stage: Mancozeb (300 g) or Captan (300 g) per 100 litres water
Fruit development stage: Bavistin + Mancozeb (25 + 250 g) per 100 litres water
15-20 days before harvest: Mancozeb (300 g) per 100 litres water
Before leaf fall: Urea (5 kg) per 100 litres water
Apple___Apple_scab.source_note: National Horticulture Board (Government of India), Apple - Diseases, citing ICAR: 50 years of crop science research in India, 1996. The PDF lists stages and fungicides as two separate columns; they are matched here in order. Open the PDF and confirm the stage-to-fungicide matching before submitting.

Apple___Black_rot.status: PARTIAL - cultural measures only; non-Indian extension sources, no doses
organic_cultural: Prune out and remove infected and dead branches (cankers) in winter
Remove and destroy mummified fruit and leaf debris to reduce infection next year
Avoid wounding branches, leaves and fruit, since open wounds are easily infected
Keep trees healthy and well watered; drought-stressed trees are infected more often
Plant resistant cultivars where available
chemical: Fungicides are rarely needed when sanitation and tree care are good. Captan and sulfur products used in scab sprays can also help protect against black rot (no dose given by the source; follow the product label and local advice)
Apple___Black_rot.source_note: University of Minnesota Extension (black rot of apple), with sanitation and pruning points from Cornell's fact sheet (blogs.cornell.edu/applevarietydatabase). Not Indian sources, and no doses given. Ask a local horticulture officer about chemicals.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.status: PARTIAL - practices and spray timing only, no doses; non-Indian source
organic_cultural: Plant resistant apple or crabapple varieties.
Remove all galls from nearby juniper/cedar before the orange telial horns form.
Removing junipers within about three miles of the orchard is said to reduce rust risk to minimum or none.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.source_note: University of Illinois Extension (Schuster and Babadoost); no date shown on page. Non-Indian source used because no Indian source on this disease was found (it needs juniper/cedar hosts, mainly North America). Page only says to start fungicide at pink flower bud stage and continue at labeled intervals until 1-2 weeks past petal-fall; it names no active ingredient or dose, so chemical is left empty. Other US extension pages list products and US label rates, not used (US-registered products, not verified for India).

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.status: PARTIAL - non-Indian extension sources, no doses
organic_cultural: Prune trees to improve air circulation; this is the best cultural control for powdery mildew
Moderate shoot growth through careful nitrogen management
chemical: Sulfur provides some control of powdery mildew (no dose given by the source; follow the product label). Fungicides are often needed only in hot, dry years
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.source_note: Michigan State University Extension, Pre-harvest disease control in cherry, with cultural points from the Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook (pnwhandbooks.org). Not Indian sources and no doses.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.disease: Cercospora leaf spot Gray leaf spot
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.status: PARTIAL - cultural only, chemical not sourced
organic_cultural: Rotate away from corn for one or two years to reduce inoculum
Select gray leaf spot resistant hybrids
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.source_note: APSnet Feature (American Phytopathological Society), not an Indian source. No TNAU/ICAR page with doses found. Chemical recommendations still needed.

organic_cultural: Remove the alternate hosts (Oxalis species)
Collect the remains of the crop and destroy by burning or burying
chemical: Foliar spray at 35 and 50 days after sowing (DAS) of ONE of: Kresoxim-methyl 44.3% SC @ 1 ml/litre, or Tebuconazole @ 1 ml/litre, or Mancozeb @ 2 ml/litre
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal, Maize common rust (Puccinia sorghi). The page also lists Chlorothalonil, but its dose is not clearly stated, so that option is left out.

organic_cultural: Burn or bury infected maize stubble
chemical: Spray Mancozeb or Zineb @ 2-4 g/litre, or Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1 ml/litre, at 35 and 50 days after sowing (DAS)
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal, Maize leaf blight (Exserohilum turcicum). A second TNAU page (maize_disease/maize_4.html) says Mancozeb or Zineb @ 2-4 g/litre at 10-day intervals after first appearance.

organic_cultural: Collect and destroy mummified berries left on the vines
Ensure free circulation of air through the vines
chemical: Spray Bordeaux mixture (4:4:100) once or twice on young bunches to prevent infection; copper fungicides are preferred on bunches because they leave no visible deposit on fruit
Grape___Black_rot.source_note: National Horticulture Board (Government of India), Grapes - Diseases, Black Rot (Guignardia bidwelli).

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).status: PARTIAL - cultural practices only, no doses; non-Indian source
organic_cultural: Use clean, healthy planting material (scion and rootstock).
Never prune vines in rainy, wet weather.
Scout the vineyard regularly; cut out infected wood at least 4 inches (as the source states) into healthy green wood and burn or bury it.
Double pruning or delayed pruning can suppress trunk diseases.
Protect pruning wounds with wound paint or protectant.
Keep vines healthy (suitable fertility, avoid over-cropping young vines); vine surgery only delays decline, so expect to remove badly diseased vines eventually.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).source_note: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, publication EPLP-034, dated 5/17 (2017). Covers grapevine trunk diseases including esca/black measles. Non-Indian source used because searches of ICAR-NRC Grapes, NHB and TNAU material found nothing on esca (the NHB page covers Dead arm/Phomopsis, a different disease). The source says complete control is virtually impossible and gives no fungicide names or doses, only 'follow the product label' for dormant sprays; chemical left empty.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.status: PARTIAL - general practices only, no doses; non-Indian source
organic_cultural: Promote vine vigor.
Improve air circulation so plant tissue dries faster (pruning, thinning, spacing, weed management).
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.source_note: University of Kentucky Scouting Guide for Problems of Fruit; undated. Page is a group page for grape leaf spots (Cercospora, Septoria, Isariopsis/Pseudocercospora, Pestalotia), not Isariopsis alone. Non-Indian source used because no Indian page on this disease was found (searched TNAU, ICAR-NRC Grapes, NHB; NRC Grapes CIB&RC list has no Isariopsis entry). It says early-season fungicides used for other diseases also help but names no product or dose, so chemical is left empty. Do not use the TNAU/ICAR ber 'black spot' (Isariopsis personata) pages; that is a different crop and pathogen.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).status: PARTIAL - one antibiotic dose only; psyllid insecticide product and dose not given by source
organic_cultural: Use pathogen-free budwood for propagation.
Control the citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri), which spreads the disease, with insecticides.
Collect and destroy damaged plant parts.
Encourage natural enemies of the psyllid such as syrphids and chrysopids.
Spray systemic insecticides during flush growth periods (source names no product or dose).
chemical: Tetracycline spray at 500 ppm, applied fortnightly (as the source states; no formulation or spray volume given)
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal, Citrus greening page (the page now has management text, unlike when first checked); no date shown. The tetracycline dose is the only dose on the page. Psyllid practices come from TNAU's separate citrus pests page (https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/crop_prot_crop_insectpest%20_-Citrus_pest&disease.html), which gives no psyllid insecticide dose; the doses on that page are for aphids, black fly and other pests and were not used. I could not confirm the tetracycline use against a CIB&RC label, so check with a local horticulture officer before use. There is no cure for the disease; removing infected trees is not mentioned by TNAU.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.status: PARTIAL - non-Indian extension source, no doses
organic_cultural: Plant bacterial spot-resistant or less susceptible varieties; this is the most sustainable control, though even resistant varieties can be infected in wet years
Fertilize trees as recommended; vigorous, well-cared-for trees are less susceptible
Sandy, windy sites and stressed trees get more bacterial spot, so choose resistant varieties there
chemical: Copper-containing sprays or oxytetracycline are used against bacterial spot; repeated applications are usually needed, and copper can injure leaves (no dose given by the source; follow the product label)
Peach___Bacterial_spot.source_note: Alabama Cooperative Extension System (Auburn University), Bacterial Spot Treatment in Peaches (ANR-2962), with spray options from Michigan State University Extension. Not Indian sources and no doses.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.status: SOURCED - TNAU chilli page (bell pepper and chilli are both Capsicum annuum)
organic_cultural: Field sanitation is important
Obtain seed from disease-free plants
chemical: Spray Mancozeb @ 2 g/litre or Copper oxychloride @ 2.5 g/litre
Seedlings may be sprayed with Bordeaux mixture 1% or Copper oxychloride 0.25%
Do not spray streptomycin after fruits begin to form
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal, Chilli bacterial leaf spot (Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria), updated Jun 2023. The page also lists a mercuric chloride seed treatment; it is left out here because mercury compounds are highly toxic.

organic_cultural: Use disease-free seed tubers for planting
Remove and destroy infected plant debris (soil spores are the primary infection source)
Variety Kufri Sindhuri has fair resistance
chemical: Very early spray with Zineb or Captan at 0.2%, repeated every 15-20 days
Potato___Early_blight.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal, potato disease page.

Potato___Late_blight.status: SOURCED - ICAR research paper (field trial result, not an official label dose)
organic_cultural: Resistant varieties in trials: Kufri Girdhari, then Kufri Himalini
Planting date affects disease: last week of April for the susceptible variety, mid-May to first week of June for resistant varieties (Nilgiris trial)
chemical: Best schedule 1: Mancozeb @ 0.2% as prophylactic first spray, then Azoxystrobin @ 0.1% as second spray
Best schedule 2: Mancozeb @ 0.2% as prophylactic first spray, then Dimethomorph + Mancozeb @ 0.3% as second spray
Continue the same sequence depending on weather, up to 75 days, at 7-10 day intervals
Potato___Late_blight.source_note: Potato Journal (ICAR), 'Management of potato late blight (Phytophthora infestans) in the Nilgiris', Vol 46(1), 2019. Checked against the abstract on the ICAR page. Nilgiris trial conditions; follow label and local agriculture officer's advice.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.status: SOURCED - TNAU muskmelon/watermelon page, which lists squash among the hosts
chemical: Wettable sulphur @ 0.2%
Squash___Powdery_mildew.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal, Muskmelon and Watermelon powdery mildew (Erysiphe cichoracearum); page has no date but a 2008-2024 copyright line. The page's symptoms text says the disease attacks muskmelons, squash, cucumbers, gourds and pumpkins, so it covers squash. Only one control is given (wettable sulphur @ 0.2%, no volume or interval stated). A squash-specific dose source (Indian Phytopathology 65(2), summer squash, ICAR epubs) was found but I only saw its listing page in search results (no abstract or doses), so it was not used.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.status: PARTIAL - cultural measures only; non-Indian extension sources, no doses
organic_cultural: Begin with clean, disease-free plant material
Use proper sanitation: remove infected leaves and plant debris
Increase air circulation so leaves dry quickly; space plants adequately
Plant new transplants frequently and control weeds
Consider resistant cultivars
chemical: Use fungicides only if the disease becomes severe (no active ingredient or dose given by these sources; ask a local agriculture officer)
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.source_note: University of Kentucky Scouting Guide (leaf scorch of strawberry), with spacing and transplant points from NC State Extension (content.ces.ncsu.edu/leaf-scorch-of-strawberry). Not Indian sources and no doses.

organic_cultural: Use disease-free seed
chemical: Streptocycline 40-100 ppm (20 g/ac)
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal (Dept. of Plant Pathology, TNAU Coimbatore); cites Crop Production Guide - Horticulture 2020.

organic_cultural: Removal and destruction of crop debris
Crop rotation
Seed treatment: Trichoderma asperellum @ 4 g/kg seeds
chemical: Iprodione 50% WP @ 600 g/ac
Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 200 ml/ac
Mancozeb 35% SC @ 1 kg/ac
Metiram 70% WG @ 1.0 kg/ac
Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 200 g/ac
Zineb 75% WP @ 800 g/ac
Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 200 ml/ac
Metiram 55% + Pyraclostrobin 5% WG @ 600 g/ac
Tebuconazole 50% + Trifloxystrobin 25% WG @ 140 g/ac
Tomato___Early_blight.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal (Dept. of Plant Pathology, TNAU Coimbatore), updated Jun 2023; cites Crop Production Guide - Horticulture 2020. Doses are per acre as given by the source.

organic_cultural: Proper drainage
Crop rotation
Soil application of Trichoderma asperellum (viride) @ 1.0 kg/ac
chemical: Cyazofamid 34.5% SC @ 80 ml/ac
Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 200 ml/ac
Mancozeb 35% SC @ 1000 g/ac
Zineb 75% WP @ 800 g/ac
Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 200 ml/ac
Tomato___Late_blight.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal (Dept. of Plant Pathology, TNAU Coimbatore); cites Crop Production Guide - Horticulture 2020. Doses are per acre as given by the source.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.status: PARTIAL - cultural only, chemical not sourced
organic_cultural: Select resistant cultivars (tolerance varies with pathogen strain)
Space plants for better air circulation and faster drying
If relative humidity exceeds 85% (greenhouse/high tunnel): open side walls or doors, turn on fans/ventilation
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.source_note: University of Kentucky Extension Plant Pathology fact sheet PPFS-VG-52 (not an Indian source; no TNAU page found). Chemical recommendations still needed from an ICAR/state agriculture university source.

organic_cultural: Removal and destruction of affected plant parts
Biological: seed treatment with Trichoderma asperellum @ 4 g/kg seeds
chemical: Fluxapyroxad 250 g/l + Pyraclostrobin 250 g/l SC @ 200-250 ml/ha
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal (Dept. of Plant Pathology, TNAU Coimbatore); cites Crop Production Guide - Horticulture 2020. Note: this dose is per hectare, others are per acre.

chemical: Spray wettable sulphur 50 WP @ 2 g/litre, or dicofol 18.5 EC @ 2.5 ml/litre
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal, Tomato red spider mite (Tetranychus spp.), updated Jun 2023. Page is for red spider mite, used here for the two-spotted spider mite class. Dicofol is an old acaricide: check that it is currently registered for use in your state before recommending it.

Tomato___Target_Spot.status: PARTIAL - fungicide types only, no doses; non-Indian source
chemical: Chlorothalonil and mancozeb gave fairly good control of target spot when applied before infection, as a preventative (no dose given by the source; follow the product label)
Strobilurin fungicides such as azoxystrobin gave excellent control in university trials (no dose given by the source; follow the product label)
Tomato___Target_Spot.source_note: University of Florida IPM, Target Spot of Tomato (Corynespora cassiicola). Not an Indian source and no doses. Fungicide resistance in this fungus has been reported, so ask a local agriculture officer for current advice.

organic_cultural: Raise nursery in protected condition
Grow sorghum, maize or bajra as barrier crop
Use disease-free seeds
Yellow sticky traps @ 5 nos./ac
Remove alternate weed host Abutilon indicum
chemical: Spray (against whitefly vector): Dimethoate 30 EC @ 200 ml/ac or Methyl demeton 25 EC @ 200 ml/ac or Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 200 g/ac or Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 200 ml/ac
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal (Dept. of Plant Pathology, TNAU Coimbatore); cites Crop Production Guide - Horticulture 2020. TNAU page is titled 'Tomato leaf curl virus'; used here for the Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus class. Chemicals target the whitefly vector, not the virus.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.status: PARTIAL - practices only; TNAU Tamil page, seed-soak dose left out because soak time is not given
organic_cultural: Select seed from healthy, disease-free plants.
Carefully remove and destroy infected plants from the field.
Do not use virus-infected seedlings for transplanting.
Rotate with crops other than tobacco, potato, chilli, capsicum and brinjal.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.source_note: TNAU Agritech Portal, Tamil-language page 'Tomato mosaic disease' (copyright 2016); I read the Tamil text and summarised it in English myself. The page does not name the virus, but its symptoms (mottling, fern-leaf) and spread by workers' clothes and hands match tomato mosaic. The page also advises soaking seed in a trisodium phosphate solution of 90 (written '90கி', gram abbreviation) per litre of water one day before sowing, then rinsing and shade-drying; this was left out because it does not say how long to soak, and a wrong soak could harm the seed. Replaces the earlier English TNAU page (tomato_diseases_12.html), which is headed Cucumber mosaic virus but lists Tomato Mosaic Virus as the cause, so its mix of CMV and ToMV details is unreliable. The page gives no insecticide or other chemical advice.
